1:
Clarke begins by repairing the join, since the act appears suspended by the unnatural division of this verse from the preceding chapter, though we may rest assured it was the immediate consequence of Jacob's death. Gill describes what the gesture was: Joseph laid his own face to the cold face and pale cheeks of his dead father, out of tender affection for him and grief at parting, which also shows that he had been present from the time his father sent for him, through the whole blessing of the tribes and the orders about the funeral. Wesley takes the kiss as an act of faith as well as of love, Joseph giving an affectionate farewell to lips already pale and cold, and supposes the rest of Jacob's sons did the same, much moved by his dying words.

Henry draws out why the grief was so heavy. Jacob was old and decrepit and must needs die in the course of nature; he was poor comparatively, and a constant charge upon his son; yet such affection had Joseph for a loving father, and so sensible was he of the loss of a prudent, pious, praying father, that he could not part with him without floods of tears. From this he takes a rule for the living: as it is an honour to die lamented, so it is the duty of survivors to lament the death of those who have been useful in their day, though for some time they may have survived their usefulness. He is careful about what the tears can and cannot reach. The departed soul is out of reach of our tears and kisses, but with them it is proper to show our respect to the poor body, of which we look for a glorious and joyful resurrection.

Calvin sorts the chapter's grief into two kinds, one natural and one ceremonial. That Joseph falls upon his father's face and sheds tears flows from true and pure affection; that the Egyptians afterwards mourn seventy days, being done for the sake of honour and in compliance with custom, is more from ostentation and vain pomp than from true grief, whence the proverb that the mourning of the heir is laughter under a mask. Even where minds are penetrated with real sorrow, he says, something is added by the affectation of making a show of pious grief, so that men weep more largely before witnesses than they would alone, and friends who meet under pretext of administering consolation often call forth more abundant weeping instead. The custom itself arose from a good principle, that the living should meditate on the curse entailed by sin upon the human race, but it has always been tarnished, being neither directed to its true end nor regulated by due moderation. Genuine grief he will not censure, and Joseph is not reproved here but commended for filial piety; yet we have need of the rein, lest through intemperate grief we be hurried by a blind impulse to murmur against God, for excessive sorrow always precipitates us into rebellion. Its mitigation, he ends, is chiefly to be sought in the hope of a future life.
2:
Gill puts the reason first: the embalming was not merely the country's custom but a necessity, since the corpse was to be carried into Canaan, which would take time. He treats the art as a branch of medicine, cites Herodotus that the Egyptians had physicians peculiar to every disease and Homer that they were the most skilful of all men, and notes that the Septuagint renders the word instead as the buriers, who took care of the burial and among the rest to embalm, dry, and roll the bodies in linen. Ellicott doubts the identification, since embalmers are not generally called physicians, and thinks the work was superintended by the physicians attached to Joseph's household; he confirms the subdivision into classes each charged with a special disease, though Maspero thinks their knowledge inconsiderable, with specialists only for the eyes and one or two similar complaints. He adds that the practice ran from two thousand years before Christ to the eighth century after, and that the bodies so preserved have been reckoned at four hundred and twenty millions. Clarke works from the words. The Hebrew for the men means the healers, whose business was to restore the body from sickness and, when death came, to preserve it from dissolution; the verb for embalming answers to an Arabic word of the same sense and is also used of the reddening of leather, so the principle may be analogous to tanning, which removes moisture and closes the pores.

The process Clarke gives from Herodotus. The embalmers show three wooden models at three prices and ask after which the dead shall be represented; the brain is drawn out through the nostrils with a crooked iron and the abdomen opened with a sharp Ethiopic stone; the bowels are cleansed with palm wine and the belly filled with myrrh and cassia; the body is salted with nitre seventy days, for longer they may not salt it, then washed and rolled in fine linen besmeared with gum and given back to the relations, who prepare a wooden coffin in the shape of a man. Clarke reckons forty days for the process and thirty more lying in natron, seventy in all. Ellicott finds the sources at variance: Herodotus gives seventy days to the embalming, but was describing Thebes, whereas Memphis was the capital in Joseph's time, and Diodorus agrees more nearly with the account here, allowing somewhat more than thirty days for it and seventy-two for the mourning of a king. Since thirty days was the usual Israelite mourning, he thinks the forty were included in the seventy. Wesley says the art was practised so curiously as to preserve the very features of the face unchanged.

Whether it should have been done at all is Calvin's question. He grants that to embalm with aromatic spices was in former times no fault, being a public symbol of future incorruption, and that burial came down from the holy fathers as a mirror of the resurrection; but hypocrites are always more diligent in ceremonies than those who possess the solid substance of things, and where faith has not breathed its odour all embalming is vapid — indeed if death be the destruction of the body it is an impious profanation to place what has perished under such costly custody. He suspects Joseph conformed from fear rather than judgment, lest his father's condition seem worse than other men's, when it would have been better to keep the frugal practice of his fathers; and on the seventy days he is sharper still, since the world affects to believe that whatever is customary is lawful, so that what prevails carries along everything it meets like a violent inundation. The mourning, he adds, was a kind of royal mourning. Wesley notices who joined it: many of the Egyptians, out of the respect they had for Joseph, put themselves into mourning for his father.
4:
Why Joseph applied through intermediaries is the first question. Clarke and Ellicott give the same answer: he was in mourning habit, and none in such dress might appear before an eastern monarch, as Esther's book shows. Ellicott adds that the mourner's dress was squalid, his beard unshorn, his hair in disorder, and that while those signs were maintained he was expected to keep to his own house. Calvin suspects a less creditable reason. Nothing was less tolerable to the Egyptians than that their land, of whose sanctity they boasted, should be despised, so Joseph put the courtiers between himself and the request and pleaded necessity, transferring the offence to his dead father by resting all on the oath. He was oppressed by servile fear and did not dare boldly to profess his own faith, whereas a more simple and upright confession is required of the sons of God. That he could not move his foot without the king's leave shows he was bound by his splendid fortune as by golden fetters, the condition of all advanced to honour in royal courts, so that nothing is better for men of sane mind than a private station.

The oath carries the plea. Gill observes that the words of dying men are always to be regarded by those who have any regard to duty and honour, much more when an oath is annexed, which among all nations was reckoned sacred. Keil corrects the verb in Jacob's account of the tomb, which means to dig, not to buy, so that Jacob attributes to himself as patriarch what had really been done by Abraham; the royal permission was needed because Joseph meant to go beyond the border with a large procession. Wesley reads the application as simple respect, since though the charge about the corn was long over Joseph was still a prime minister of state and would not be so long absent without licence. Calvin thinks Pharaoh may have been moved by the modesty of the manner, though it was God who influenced the proud mind of the king; and he notices what respect for an oath prevailed among blind unbelievers, since Pharaoh had not sworn and still deemed it unlawful to violate by his own authority a pledge given by another, whereas now men count it a trifle to deceive under God's name.

The procession drew comment from all. Keil explains the route, that it did not take the shortest way by Gaza through the Philistines' country, probably because so large a company with a military escort would meet difficulties there, but went round by the Dead Sea. Clarke likens the elders of the house to the Aldermen of our Saxon ancestors, and sets the whole against a modern state funeral: here was no conqueror, no mighty man of valour, no person of proud descent, but a plain man who had dwelt almost all his life in tents, with no subjects but his cattle, honoured with a national mourning. If it be said this was all done out of respect to Joseph, why was Joseph so respected? Not because he had conquered nations or made his sword drunk with blood, but because he had saved men alive. Henry finds the fuller description deliberate, since Jacob had spoken more than once of dying for grief and going to the grave bereaved of his children, and behold, he dies in honour, followed by all of them; the Egyptians who had looked on the Hebrews with disdain now knew them better, good old Jacob having so conducted himself as to gain universal esteem. Calvin will not excuse the tumultuous clamour, and thinks even the seven days an excess, yet sees why God allowed it: had Jacob been buried privately his fame would soon have been extinguished, whereas now a sublime trophy stands before men's eyes to cherish the hope of the promised inheritance.
8:
Gill lists the company: Joseph with his two sons and servants, his eleven brethren and such of their sons as were grown, and as many of his father's domestics as could be spared. Ellicott notes that the word for the great company is properly camp, and that the Egyptian elders were chief officers of Pharaoh's household and of the districts into which the country was divided; on the Israelite side only the men of rank went, the dependents remaining with the cattle in Goshen. Gill gives two reasons for the chariots and horsemen, honour and grandeur, and safety, in case they were set upon by robbers or opposed by the Canaanites and refused the cave of Machpelah. Ellicott finds the same caution in the route. The march went round the east of the Dead Sea rather than the shorter ways, since the wilderness of Judah was difficult and the path above Engedi so steep that a few Amorites might have held it against any number, probably impracticable for chariots; the Philistine road was easy, but hostilities are recorded between the sons of Joseph and the Philistines, and he would not expose his father's remains to attack.

The halting-place is disputed in name and position. Clarke says the word means a bramble, so the Arabic takes it for a place, though all the other versions and the Targums make it a man's name; and since threshing-floors were always in the open field, Atad was probably a great farmer or the chief of a clan. Gill reports the other derivation, that the floor was hedged about with thorns to preserve it, and passes on Jerome's location three miles from Jericho and two from Jordan, called in his day Bethagla, the place of a circuit, because there they went about like mourners. Ellicott observes that with agriculture only beginning in Canaan such a floor would be common property, and places Goren-Atad at Beth-Hoglah between the Jordan and Jericho. On the name he finds a play of the kind always dear to Orientals: the words for mourning and for meadow differ only in a vowel, and since the versions were made before the points were affixed they all read the mourning of Egypt, where the Hebrew text as now pointed has the meadow of Egypt. Wesley takes the name as a standing testimony against the next generation of Egyptians, who oppressed the posterity of the Jacob to whom their ancestors showed such respect. Keil thinks the Egyptian procession stopped here, since only Jacob's sons are named as carrying him into Canaan.

Clarke turns the seven days into an argument. Hebrew mourning was ordinarily seven days and by exception thirty, never longer, the seventy being Egyptian and forced by the embalming; man, wiser in his own estimation than the word of God, has added eleven whole months, which nature itself pronounces absurd, since it cannot sustain grief so long, so that mourning is now a grave mimicry and a vain show convicting itself of hypocrisy. Of the burial little is said. Gill is careful that his sons carried him means they saw to it, not that they bore him on their shoulders as the devout men bore Stephen; Clarke notes that Locke and others would attach these two verses to the close of the previous chapter, where they read more consistently. Calvin asks why they all went back. They had left pledges enough in Egypt to require it, but he thinks they were drawn rather by the oracle given to Abraham, that his seed should be a stranger in a land not theirs and be afflicted there, which the fathers left their sons as a precious treasure; they returned because it was not lawful to shake off the yoke God had laid on their necks, and a special sense of religion subdued men whose temper was not otherwise mild enough to bear lighter burdens.
15:
Gill reads the seeing as an act of the mind rather than the eye: they considered that their father was dead and buried, that they had lost an affectionate parent concerned for the peace of all his family, and that what turn things would now take they did not know. Ellicott renders the fear as a question, what if Joseph should hate us, and notes that they had seen no change in his treatment of them, only that if he cherished revenge they were now in his power. Keil finds the sentence broken off before its end, an aposiopesis presupposing a case not desired and for the present not real, though perhaps possible. Clarke takes it as evidence of guilt rather than danger, since conscience records criminality and, breeding continual fears, destroys all peace of mind; he quotes Juvenal in Dryden's version, that though bribes or favour pronounce a man guiltless, none quits himself, his own impartial thought will damn him. Henry and Wesley say the same briefly: while their father lived they thought themselves safe under his shadow, and a guilty conscience exposes men to continual frights, so that those who would be fearless must keep themselves guiltless. Calvin presses the injustice. They judged Joseph by their own disposition, imagining that respect for his father alone had made him postpone revenge, which wronged a man whose liberality had borne witness that his mind was free from hatred, and wronged God too, whose grace had shone in that moderation. He had absolved them already; they became their own tormentors.

The embassy itself puzzles them. Gill rejects the guesses that Bilhah or her sons were sent, and thinks the messengers were of their own number, likely Judah and Benjamin — Benjamin as having had no part in the selling and being his brother by both parents, Judah as having saved his life when the rest were for shedding his blood. Clarke will not decide whether Jacob left such a charge; some think the story feigned, which he judges unlikely, since Jacob may have had his own suspicions and thought it best that his sons humble themselves and get a fresh assurance of forgiveness. Calvin thinks the device foolish. If Jacob had been anxious, why did he not reconcile them himself while he lived, and why attempt through mediators what they could have done better in person? The Lord suffers them to act like children, that we may learn to expect nothing from frivolous inventions. He guesses the messengers were domestic servants, since it would have been folly to publish such infamy among the Egyptians.

The plea is heaped up rather than argued. Calvin observes that they do not extenuate the fault but freely charge themselves with guilt, setting against the atrocity of the crime their father's authority and then the sacred name of God; the confession would have deserved commendation had they come directly instead of by tortuous contrivances. From the title they take he draws a rule: if we are injured by members of the Church we must not be rigid and immovable in pardoning, for where the bond of religion is added we are harder than iron if not inclined to compassion. Clarke thinks the words wonderfully well chosen and spoken in the most forcible manner to Joseph's piety and filial affection, so no wonder he wept. Wesley explains the title: they were not only children of the same Jacob but worshippers of the same Jehovah, and such we should always treat with peculiar tenderness, since we and they have the same master. On the weeping he distinguishes two sorts of tears, sorrow that they should suspect him and tenderness at their submission. Calvin will not have the scene staged, as some suppose: learning from the messengers how their minds were tormented, Joseph was moved with sympathy, sent for them, and their own deprecating speech drew the tears.
18:
Gill notes that the messengers' return gave them courage to come from Goshen themselves. Ellicott takes the answer as a refusal of the judge's office, judges being sometimes called God in Hebrew as exercising his authority. Clarke allows the words to be either question or affirmation: read one way Joseph has passed the transgression by and the matter lies between them and God; read the other, he stands in God's place as a distributor of his bounty, and will nourish not only them but their little ones. Wesley hears humility rather than office, Joseph thinking they showed him too much respect and answering as Peter did Cornelius, stand up, I myself also am a man; make your peace with God and you will find it easy to make your peace with me. Calvin sifts the readings and rejects most. Joseph is not refusing the honour, since he often let himself be addressed so; nor declining to punish in hope that God will avenge; nor merely observing that the affair was God's doing, though that comes nearer the truth. Since the Hebrew particle can mean under, the sentence would read but for its interrogative as fear not, for I am under God; as it stands it means a mortal may not presume to thwart the counsel of God. Joseph restrains his feelings as with a bridle, and nothing assuages anger better than submitting to be governed by God.

On the sentence that follows they agree. Gill will not let the intention be softened: they meant to contradict his dreams, take away his life, or at least make him a slave all his days. Ellicott points out that the verb is the same in both clauses, so man's purpose is set against God's in one word, and that the great people saved are the Egyptians. Wesley adds that the evil made Joseph a greater blessing to his family than he could otherwise have been. Calvin uses the verse to separate two things in one act. The selling was a crime detestable for its cruelty and perfidy, yet he was not sold except by the decree of heaven; God did not merely stay at rest and slacken the reins of human malice to use the occasion afterwards, but appointed the order of acting himself. It was not for that a work common to both, since while they contrived their brother's destruction God was effecting their deliverance from on high, and whatever poison Satan produces God turns to medicine for his elect. Where our minds cannot reach such depths, he says, let them adore what they do not comprehend rather than, as vessels of clay, exalt themselves against their Maker.

The promise of maintenance is the test of the reconciliation. Ellicott notes that the little ones are the word rendered households by the Greek and families by the Syriac, meaning dependents. Calvin makes the point sharply: it is a token of solid and not feigned reconciliation not merely to abstain from malice but to overcome evil with good, and most weakly conclude they have forgiven an offence if they do not retaliate, as if withdrawing our hands from help were not itself a revenge. You would assist your brother if you thought him worthy; he implores your aid, and you desert him because he has done you some unkindness — what hinders you but hatred? On speaking to their heart he observes that Joseph removed all their scruples by addressing them with suavity and kindness. Wesley admires the manner as much as the substance. Joseph did not tell them they were upon their good behaviour and that he would be kind if they carried themselves well; he would not hold them in suspense, nor seem jealous of them though they had been suspicious of him. Those we love and forgive, he concludes, we must not only do well for, but speak kindly to.
22:
Gill sums the years quietly: Joseph dwelt in Egypt comfortably and in great prosperity, and not he only, but his brethren and their families, as long as he lived. Clarke measures the same clause forward, since his father's house means all the descendants of Israel, who continued there until the departure under Moses and Aaron a hundred and forty-four years later. Henry reads the length of the life as a reward attached to a commandment: having honoured his father, Joseph's days were long in the land which for the present God had given him, and it was a great mercy to his relations that God continued him so long, a support and comfort to them.

Calvin finds the constancy more remarkable than the length. Raised to great honour and power among the Egyptians, Joseph remained closely united to his father's house, and gradually took his leave of the treasures of the court, thinking there was nothing better to do than hold them in contempt, lest earthly dignity should separate him from the kingdom of God. He went further than that, descending to an ignoble condition on purpose and weaning his own sons from any hope of succeeding to his rank. We know how anxiously other men labour that they may not be reduced in circumstances and may leave their fortune entire to their posterity; Joseph spent sixty years bringing himself and his children into a state of submission, lest his earthly greatness should alienate them from the little flock of the Lord. He imitated the serpents, which cast off their slough that, being stripped of their old age, they may gather new strength. He would rather see his descendants devoted to a pastoral life and despised by the Egyptians, if only they might be reckoned in the family of Israel. And in so numerous an offspring during his own lifetime the Lord gave him some taste of his blessing, from which he might conceive the hope of the deliverance to come, for among so many temptations he needed sustaining lest he sink.

The children he lived to see are counted precisely. Ellicott makes the third generation Joseph's great-grandchildren, and instances Eran, the son of Shuthelah and grandson of Ephraim, as one born in his lifetime. Gill draws a conclusion from the fact, that Jacob's prediction of Ephraim's greatness and numbers had very early begun to take effect. On the phrase about the knees Ellicott is careful: the Hebrew says they were born upon Joseph's knees, which means that he adopted them, though they would not form tribes, that prerogative being reserved for the sons of Jacob, but would count as his sons and form families. Clarke takes the same phrase practically, that they were educated by him or under his direction, his sons and their children continuing to acknowledge him as the head of the family as long as he lived. Henry adds what such a sight is worth to an old man, since it contributes much to the comfort of aged parents to see their posterity in a flourishing condition, especially if with it they see peace upon Israel.
24:
Gill sets the scene: some time before the end Joseph called them together and said he expected to die shortly. Clarke reads the promise as pointing past the present comfort of Egypt: God will yet give them, when it is essentially necessary, the most signal proof of his love; they have here everything that can make life comfortable, but this is not the land given by covenant, which represents the rest remaining for the people of God. Wesley draws the pastoral use. Jacob had spoken to the same purpose, and so must we comfort others with the comforts wherewith we have been comforted of God; Joseph had been under God both protector and benefactor of his brethren, and what would become of them now? God's gracious visits make up the loss of our best friends; and they must not settle in Egypt, but set their hearts on the land of promise and call that home. Ellicott notes what the sentence accomplishes: it is the proof of Joseph's faith commended in Hebrews, and the preparation for the next book, so that his faith joins the two.

Calvin asks why Joseph alone is recorded as leaving such a charge. He grants that the other patriarchs probably gave the same command, all their bones being conveyed into Canaan. Joseph is singled out for two reasons: the eyes of all were fixed on him for his high authority, so it was his duty to lead the way and beware lest the splendour of his dignity cast a stumbling block before them; and it mattered as an example that the man who held second place in Egypt should be content with a portion which was only that of the heir of a bare promise. He then asks where the certainty came from, since we do not read that God appeared to Joseph or an angel brought an oracle. It came from his father: being persuaded that Jacob was a divinely appointed teacher and prophet, he relied on that testimony as securely as if a vision had been given him. Unless the hearing of the word suffices for our faith, he adds, we do not deserve that God should deal with us; and this restrains those who, desiring visions, despise the ordinary ministry of the Church.

The oath binds more than those who swore it. Gill observes that it was taken not of the brethren only but of their posterity, as many as were grown, so that it might reach the generation that departed out of Egypt. Clarke traces the sequel: their descendants held themselves bound, Moses took the body at the departure, and Joshua buried it at Shechem, in the portion Jacob had bought from the Amorites. He reads the charge as Hebrews does, an act of faith made when dying, and thinks Joseph regarded these things as typical, expressing by it his belief in the immortality of the soul and the resurrection. Calvin hears an admission that the exile would feel like oblivion, as if God had turned his back for a season, and yet Joseph fixes his mind's eye on God, like the prophet waiting on the Lord that hideth his face from the house of Jacob; his choice of a sepulchre was a seal of redemption, the bones being relics whose sight declared that the eternal covenant had not died with the men who carried it. Keil notes that the body was laid in the ordinary coffin of sycamore wood and deposited in a room, as Egyptian custom required, where it stayed three hundred and sixty years until the exodus. Wesley puts the choice as a comparison. In Egypt they buried their great men with much pomp, and Joseph prefers a plain burial in Canaan, deferred almost two hundred years, to a magnificent one where he lay; he dies in Egypt, but lays his bones at stake that God will visit Israel.
26:
Gill dates the death from more than one quarter: the age is the exact number assigned by Polyhistor out of Demetrius, a heathen writer, the Jewish writers say Joseph died first of the twelve patriarchs though he was the youngest of them, and Ussher places it in the year of the world 2369. Clarke reads the Hebrew idiom, which calls him the son of a hundred and ten years, as a figure by which the period of life is personified, all the years of which it was composed represented as a nurse or father feeding and supporting him to the end — the figure rhetoricians call prosopopoeia, which is very frequent in Scripture. On the embalming he notes that the same precautions were taken as for Jacob, and that they were particularly necessary here, since this body had to last a hundred and forty-four years, the length of the bondage after Joseph's death.

The coffin draws more comment than the death. Clarke observes that with us the poorest people have coffins, the parish paying if the relations cannot, whereas in the east they are not always used even now; the ancient Jews seem to have buried without them, since neither our Lord's body nor Elisha's was so enclosed, the bones of the latter being touched by a corpse let down into his sepulchre. In Egypt they were used, and antique cases of stone and of sycamore wood survive, besides those of cloth folded and glued many times, plastered and painted with hieroglyphics. Because this was an Egyptian custom and not the practice of the neighbouring countries, he thinks the historian deliberately records that Joseph was not only embalmed but coffined. Nor were they for everyone: Maillet reports that most bodies in those chambers were simply embalmed and swathed and laid side by side without ceremony, some so slightly embalmed that nothing remains in the linen but half-rotten bones, and that the niches were designed for the heads of families, so that a coffin marks the honour the Egyptians did Joseph in death as in life. Ellicott says the word means a case or chest of wood, the mummy-cases being generally sycamore, and Gill describes the Egyptian practice of standing such a chest against a wall.

Where it stood afterwards is guessed rather than known. Gill thinks Goshen most likely, in the keeping of some of Joseph's posterity, and reports Leo Africanus placing the burial in the Heracleotic nome, from which Moses dug him up. Ellicott gives the reason for keeping the body near: with their great protector gone the Israelites could not have gone up to Hebron with a military escort, so the embalmed body was to lie where it could easily be removed when the deliverance came, and the wish was fulfilled when Moses took the bones and Joshua buried them at Shechem. Wesley draws the lesson from the long delay, that if the soul does but return to its rest with God the matter is not great though the deserted body find its rest in the grave late or not at all; yet care ought to be taken of the bodies of the saints, in the belief of their resurrection, for there is a covenant with the dust which shall be remembered, and a commandment was given concerning these bones. Ellicott closes the book with a survey. With this death ends the preparation for the forming of a chosen race: in Palestine, where Abraham had wandered as a stranger, the family could never have multiplied, the peoples there being too powerful to permit it, so that Abraham and Lot, and Esau and Jacob, had been forced apart; now under Joseph they were settled in a large, fertile and almost uninhabited region among men of their own stock, and when we next read of them they had grown into a people so vast that Egypt was afraid of them.
